notes.1b: (i) Some candidates expressed the idea that the material used to hang the limestone from the stand should have a high melting point. A significant number of candidates incorrectly suggested materials that would burn or melt such as string, rubber bands and nylon.
notes.1bii: Candidates that had experienced the use of a Bunsen burner were able to state that the air hole should be open. A large number of responses showed a lack of knowledge and understanding of a Bunsen burner.
notes.1c: (i) This question was generally well answered.
notes.1cii: Many candidates realised that solution A was limewater and scored credit for the effect of passing carbon dioxide through limewater. �PAGE�41
notes.2a: A significant number of candidates incorrectly drew lines of best fit which included the anomalous point. Some candidates failed to use a ruler.
notes.2b: Reasons for the anomalous point were often vague.
notes.2c: This question was generally well answered. Most candidates were able to extrapolate the graph and record the energy value for n = 6. Some candidates misread the scale on the y-axis.
notes.2d: This question was often poorly attempted. Some answers failed to give the energy values; other answers gave incorrect values and only scored partial credit.
notes.3a: The vast majority of candidates gave electrolysis as the process involved.
notes.3b: The majority of candidates correctly identified the expected observations. Comments which did not refer to observations were ignored.
notes.3c: Candidates who performed well correctly specified platinum as a suitable metal for the inert metal electrodes. References to unsuitable metals, such as iron and copper, were prevalent and scored no credit. Graphite and carbon were common incorrect answers.
notes.3d: The test for oxygen was well known.
notes.3e: The majority of candidates realised that hydrogen formed at the negative electrode.
notes.3f: Only the better-performing candidates realised that chlorine gas would be formed, which is a toxic gas. A frequently occurring wrong answer referred to the hazards of concentrated hydrochloric acid. A lack of practical experience was shown by some candidates who discussed flammability and the dangers of repeating the experiment.
notes.4d: The table of results was usually completed correctly and many candidates scored full credit.
notes.4e: The majority of candidates correctly plotted the results and drew a smooth line graph. Some 3 3 candidates plotted the point for the concentration 1.0 mol / dm at 0.1 mol / dm .
notes.4f: (i) This question was well answered although some candidates did not show clearly on the graph how the answer was worked out.
notes.4fii: Most candidates scored credit for extrapolating the curve to the y-axis to show the time expected using sulfuric acid of concentration of 1.2 mol / dm .
notes.4g: The idea of a fair test or comparability of results was well understood by candidates.
notes.4h: This question was well answered. Candidates had no difficulty using the thermometer diagrams to record the two temperatures.
notes.4iii: Better-performing candidates realised that half the value of magnesium used would result in half the temperature change.
notes.4j: Many responses indicated that candidates had not read the question carefully because many candidates did not suggest a different method. Good answers described using a gas syringe or thermometer to measure the volumes of gas evolved or the temperature changes over time respectively. �PAGE�42

notes.6: The quality of responses to this question was extremely broad. Most candidates scored some credit for taking a measured weight of the toothpaste and adding water to it. Some incorrect responses discussed filtering the toothpaste which would not work. Others candidates suggested heating the toothpaste, incorrectly thinking that the water and the sodium fluoride would evaporate. Likewise, methods involving the formation of sodium fluoride crystals showed a lack of knowledge and understanding of practical work involving insoluble substances. Well-planned answers from better-performing candidates gave the essential experimental details with a clear practical method and means of separating the calcium carbonate from the toothpaste and purifying the sample. The best responses also indicated how to carry out the calculations to find the percentage of calcium carbonate in the toothpaste from their experimental results. �PAGE�43
notes.key_messages:
Questions requiring candidates to plan an investigation should be answered with details of the apparatus to
be used. The practical procedures should be clearly specified and candidates should provide a conclusion.
Candidates are advised to write preliminary notes before starting to write the plan.
Candidates should use a sharp pencil for plotting points and for drawing lines of best fit on their graphs. The
line of best fit might be a curve or a straight line. Straight lines should be drawn with a ruler, but rulers should
not be used to join the points on a curve. Lines of best fit should avoid anomalous points.
notes.general_comments:
The majority of candidates attempted all of the questions. Some candidates showed a lack of experience
with and knowledge of practical procedures.
Candidates found Questions 1, 2, 4(j) and 6 to be the most demanding.
